bib.title: ChatDB: Augmenting LLMs with Databases as Their Symbolic Memory

question: Can a database manipulated by an LLM through SQL serve as symbolic memory that supports multi-hop reasoning and avoids error accumulation better than prompt-held history?
hypothesis: Symbolic memory (SQL database) with chain-of-memory improves multi-hop reasoning and precise calculation over conventional neural/prompt memory.
contributions: Propose augmenting LLMs with databases as external symbolic memory, enabling symbolic operations via SQL.
Chain-of-memory approach converts user input into multi-step intermediate memory operations.
Experiments show symbolic memory improves multi-hop reasoning and prevents error accumulation, significantly outperforming ChatGPT on a synthetic dataset.

method.summary: An LLM controller (GPT-3.5 Turbo) turns each record or question into a chain of SQL statements run on MySQL; later steps may be rewritten from earlier SQL results (chain-of-memory), then the LLM summarises a reply. Compared with GPT-3.5 Turbo given all 70 records in its prompt on a 50-question synthetic fruit-shop set.
method.task: Record keeping and question answering over a synthetic fruit shop history (multi-hop reasoning, arithmetic)

datasets.name: Fruit Shop Dataset (synthetic)
datasets.size: 70 records, approximately 3.3k tokens; 50 questions (15 easy, 35 hard) with annotated standard answers
datasets.source: Synthesised by the authors; records cover purchasing, selling, changing prices, goods returns, all valid (no negative inventory), in chronological order
datasets.preprocessing: ChatDB: records processed one by one into the database; database schema generated manually or with LLMs. Baseline: records placed in the prompt

inference.samples: each question independently answered by each model; number of runs and seeds not stated
inference.prompting: ChatDB: in-context exemplars of several chain-of-memory step sequences plus chain-of-thought prompting (exemplars not printed). Baseline: single prompt with records and question (Fig 4).
inference.retrieval: None for baseline (full records in prompt); ChatDB reads via SQL SELECT

parameters.chain_of_memory: LLM decides per step whether to update the next SQL operation based on earlier SQL results (Algorithm 1)

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: Fraction of the 50 questions answered correctly against annotated standard answers, reported for easy (15), hard (35) and all (50); who or what judged correctness is not stated

baselines: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 Turbo) with all records in prompt
eval.protocol: Single evaluation, no seeds, no significance test, no stated grader.

availability.code: Project website https://chatdatabase.github.io/ (code availability not stated in text)

prompts.purpose: Baseline ChatGPT question answering on Fruit Shop Dataset
prompts.text:
Suppose you are a fruit shop manager and good at analyzing history records.
The fruit shop newly opened on January 1, 2023. Given the history records for the fruit shop in January 2023, which include customer names, transaction dates, fruit prices, quantities purchased, and whether the items were returned, you need to answer some questions.
By default, exclude the sales transactions that have been returned when performing calculations.
Here are the historical records of the fruit shop, which are arranged in chronological order based on the occurrence time, surrounded by triple backticks:
```
{records}
```
Based on the history records, answer the question about the fruit shop:
{question}

evidence.quote: we simply treat them as part of the prompt

results.claim: ChatDB answered 41 of 50 questions correctly (82%) against 11 of 50 (22%) for ChatGPT with the records in its prompt.
results.setup: Fruit Shop Dataset, 70 records ~3.3k tokens, 50 questions, GPT-3.5 Turbo temperature 0 both systems, MySQL, single evaluation
results.table: Table 2, row ChatDB (ours), columns All 41/50 and Accuracy 82%; row ChatGPT 11/50, 22%

results.claim: On the 35 hard (multi-hop) questions ChatDB got 28 right against 1 for ChatGPT.
results.table: Table 2, row ChatDB (ours), column Hard 28/35; row ChatGPT 1/35

results.claim: On the 15 easy questions ChatDB got 13 right against 10 for ChatGPT.
results.table: Table 2, row ChatDB (ours), column Easy 13/15; row ChatGPT 10/15

results.claim: The dataset was deliberately kept within ChatGPT's token limit so the baseline needs no memory; authors infer ChatDB would beat memory-augmented ChatGPT at larger scale (argued, not measured).
results.quote: if ChatDB outperforms ChatGPT when the dataset is small, it indicates that ChatDB is also superior to memory-augmented ChatGPT when the dataset is large.

results.claim: Authors assert ChatDB's performance is unaffected by dataset length and in theory handles unlimited records (no experiment).
results.quote: in theory, ChatDB can handle an infinite number of historical records without sacrificing performance.

results.claim: Qualitative: ChatGPT errs in per-sale arithmetic, misses valid transactions, hits the max token length; ChatDB delegates arithmetic to SQL.
results.setup: Figure 5, three hand-picked example questions requiring one, two, three chain-of-memory steps
results.quote: While ChatGPT fails to answer any of the questions correctly, ChatDB successfully answers all of them.

limits: Single synthetic dataset built by the authors, 50 questions, one evaluation with no seeds, variance or significance test.
Only baseline is ChatGPT with full records in the prompt; no vector-retrieval memory, MemGPT or other memory baselines run.
Claim that vector-similarity memory is error-prone and that ChatDB scales to long histories is argued, not measured.
Who graded answers is not stated; ChatDB's exemplar prompts and database schema are not printed.

terms.definition: transforms user input into a series of intermediate memory operation steps that lead to final results
memory stored in a database and manipulated by executing SQL statements generated by an LLM

lineage.note: CoM seen as augmenting CoT with symbolic memory
Text-to-SQL, differs in treating DB as memory

lineage.work: Memory augmented LLMs are computationally universal (Schuurmans)
